extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors, patent attorneys, and patent examiners working on U.S. Section 101 subject-matter eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and drafting patent claims for subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the USPTO 2019 Revised Guidance and October update (Alice/Mayo framework). Intended to inform prosecution strategy and examiner rejections under Step 2A/2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify specific limitation considered directed to abstract concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify specific limitation that is considered directed to abstract concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations must be mapped to one of three Enumerated Groupings. Examiners should identify the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception rather than treating an entire claim generically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map limitations to Enumerated Groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations must be mapped to one of three Enumerated Groupings (mathematical concepts; certain methods of organizing human activity; mental processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the enumerated groupings rather than relying on case-by-case comparisons. The 2019 PEG shifts examiners' focus to these groupings, which synthesize Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent, to produce consistent results across technologies and claim types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim 'recites' a judicial exception (Step 2A – Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether claim recites a judicial exception. A claim 'recites' a judicial exception when the judicial exception is 'set forth' or 'described' in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set forth: claims clearly state the judicial exception (e.g., explicitly state a mathematical equation). Describe: the concept can be identified even if not explicitly named (e.g., recitation of intermediated settlement without using those words). Distinct claim elements can be treated separately, but examiners should not inappropriately parse claims; consider limitations together to avoid separate abstract-idea calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts include mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mathematical relationship is a relationship between variables or numbers and may be expressed in words or symbols. A claim reciting a numerical formula or equation falls within this grouping; textual formulas may also fall within it. 'Determining' a variable or 'performing' a mathematical operation may be considered mathematical calculations when the broadest reasonable interpretation encompasses a mathematical calculation. Examiners should consider whether a claim actually recites a mathematical concept or merely includes limitations based on or involving mathematical concepts; claims do not recite a mathematical concept if it is only based on or involves mathematical concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: This grouping covers certain methods of organizing human activity, limited to specified sub-groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'certain' is important: not all methods of organizing human activity are abstract ideas (e.g., a defined set of steps for combining ingredients to make a drug formulation is not). The grouping is limited to sub-groupings: (1) fundamental economic principles or practices (hedging, insurance, mitigating risk), (2) commercial or legal interactions (agreements, contracts, legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales activities, business relations), and (3) managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people (social activities, teaching, following rules). The grouping is not generally to be expanded beyond these sub-groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental processes are concepts performed in the human mind (including observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims do not recite a mental process when they contain limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind (e.g., mind is not equipped). Claims can recite a mental process even if performed on a computer. Use of a physical aid (pen and paper) to help perform a mental step does not negate the mental nature of the limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A – Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the identified judicial exception is integrated into a practical application (i.e., the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key considerations include whether the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or other technology and whether the specification provides sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement. Test for practical application: (1) evaluate the specification to see if the disclosure shows an improvement (the specification need not explicitly state the improvement but it must be apparent to a person of ordinary skill; conclusory assertions are insufficient); (2) ensure the claim reflects the disclosed improvement by including components or steps that provide the improvement (the claim need not explicitly state 'thereby increasing X' to reflect the improvement). Improvements in the judicial exception itself (e.g., a better economic concept) do not count as improvements in technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying judicial exception to particular treatment or prophylaxis (medical claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim can integrate a judicial exception into a practical application by applying or using the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for practical application in this context: (1) Particularity — the treatment or prophylaxis must be 'particular' and not encompass all applications of the exception; (2) Relationship — the treatment/prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the exception(s); (3) Not extra-solution or field-of-use — the limitation must impose meaningful limits and cannot be mere extra-solution activity or a field-of-use restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significantly more analysis (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether claim elements beyond the judicial exception, individually and in combination, amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application under Step 2A Prong Two, consider whether the additional elements provide 'significantly more' under Step 2B. The examiner should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO examiner's duty to establish a prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: For a 101 rejection, the examiner must explain and support each step of the 101 analysis (Step 2A Prong One, Step 2A Prong Two, and Step 2B) to establish a prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2A Prong One: the rejection should identify the judicial exception by referring to what is recited (set forth or described) in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception. No requirement exists for the examiner to provide additional external support (publications, affidavits) for the conclusion that a claim recites a judicial exception. Step 2A Prong Two: the rejection should identify additional elements beyond the exception and evaluate integration into a practical application using the PEG considerations, explaining that either there are no additional elements or that those elements do not integrate the exception. Step 2B: the examiner should explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and interpretation of examples and case law
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of hypothetical examples and the shift from case-comparison to enumerated groupings in the 2019 PEG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are illustrative and should be interpreted based on their fact patterns; a claim need not mirror an example to be eligible. The October update steers examiners away from direct case-by-case comparisons toward applying the enumerated groupings synthesized from Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent. The PEG's examples facilitate consistent examination across technologies, but different fact patterns may yield different outcomes; analyze claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting tips to support practical application and avoid 101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical drafting and prosecution strategies to improve chances of surviving a 101 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continue to review disclosures critically and use a technical problem/technical solution approach. Include additional language/discussion in the specification that helps support the 'practical application' (ensure practical application dovetails with the technical solution). During prosecution: interview every 101 rejection (many examiners will withdraw 101 rejections after interviews), be prepared to walk through the entire Revised Guidance analysis with the examiner, and include arguments addressing both the revised guidelines (PEG) and relevant case law.
